definition: A nickname for a system with no recognisable structure, where every part depends on every other part, so any change is risky. The term comes from a 1997 paper by Brian Foote and Joseph Yoder.

The observation, from Melvin Conway in 1968, that organisations which design systems tend to produce designs that copy their own communication structure. Teams that rarely talk tend to end up with components joined by awkward interfaces.
example: Four separate teams building a compiler tend to produce a four-pass compiler.

definition: Deliberately shaping team structure to match the architecture you want, using Conway's law in reverse. If you want an independent search service, you create a team that owns search end to end.
Martin Fowler's advice to start a new system as a well-structured monolith, learn where the real boundaries are, and only then extract services when there is a concrete reason.

A way to replace an old system gradually: put a routing layer in front, rebuild one capability at a time behind it, shift traffic to the new part, then retire the old code. Named after a fig that grows around a host tree and eventually replaces it.
example: Route /billing/* to a new Billing service while everything else still goes to the monolith.

definition: An approach to software design, described by Eric Evans in 2003, that models code closely on the business domain and its language, and splits large systems into bounded contexts.
Something the business does to create value, such as taking orders, billing or managing inventory. Service boundaries are often drawn around business capabilities rather than technical layers.
How closely the parts inside one module or service belong together. High cohesion means most changes for a feature stay inside one unit.
How much one module or service depends on another. With tight coupling, a change or failure in one forces changes or failures in the other; loose coupling lets them change and fail independently.
A dependency in time: the caller only succeeds if the service it calls is up and responding at that same moment. Synchronous calls create it; asynchronous messaging removes it.
Collecting the logs from every service and instance into one searchable store, usually tagged with request or trace IDs so you can follow one request across services.
Testing that two services agree on the shape and meaning of the messages they exchange (the contract), without running both together. It catches breaking API changes before deployment.
A team that builds and runs shared infrastructure (deployment pipelines, observability, service mesh, Kubernetes clusters) so that product teams can ship services without each rebuilding it.

A code editor bundled with tools such as refactoring, debugging and code navigation, for example IntelliJ IDEA or Visual Studio Code. Renaming a function everywhere is one IDE operation inside a monolith.
A fixed, shared release schedule that every team's changes must join. It forces teams to coordinate and wait for each other.
When two people change the same lines of code in different branches and version control cannot combine them automatically, so someone must resolve it by hand.
A web application framework written in the Ruby programming language. Shopify and GitHub run very large Rails applications.
An open-source tool built by Shopify that checks a Ruby application's code for references that cross declared package boundaries, used to enforce a modular monolith.
A large programming question-and-answer website, often cited as an example of very high traffic served by a small number of monolithic servers.
The executive responsible for a company's technology and engineering.

Replacing a whole system in one switch-over after building the replacement separately. It concentrates risk at a single cut-over day, which is why incremental approaches such as the strangler fig are usually preferred.
The moment traffic or writes are switched from an old system or index to a new one.
Deploying a new version by replacing instances a few at a time, so the service keeps running throughout. Kubernetes Deployments do this by default.
A load-balancing rule that picks a server from a hash of the client's IP address, so the same client keeps landing on the same server.
Making an issued token stop working before its expiry. Self-contained tokens such as JWTs cannot be revoked without some server-side check, such as a denylist.
Describes work whose speed is limited by waiting for input/output (disk, network or another service) rather than by the processor. I/O-bound servers can be overloaded while their CPU looks idle.
How long the oldest message has been waiting in a queue. It shows directly how far behind consumers are, which queue length alone does not.

A lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL. In transaction pooling mode it lends a real server connection to a client only for the length of one transaction, so many clients share few connections; session-level features then behave differently.
The PostgreSQL setting that caps how many client connections the server accepts; extra connection attempts are refused with an error. Changing it needs a server restart.
A packaged, read-only snapshot of an application and its dependencies from which containers are started. Images are immutable, so you replace containers rather than patch them.
Software that schedules containers onto machines, restarts them when they fail, scales them and connects them to the network. Kubernetes is the most widely used.
A Kubernetes component that repeatedly compares the cluster's actual state with the desired state and acts to close the gap, such as starting pods until the replica count matches.
A Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of identical pods (replicas) running from a template, and replaces them gradually during a rolling update or rollback.
Kubernetes APIs that route external HTTP traffic into the cluster to Services, based on host names and paths. Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor to Ingress.
The Kubernetes controller that changes a Deployment's replica count from metrics such as average CPU. It asks for the replica count that would bring the metric back to its target, rounded up.
example: 4 pods at 90% CPU with a 60% target scale to 6 pods.

definition: The band around the target in which the HorizontalPodAutoscaler does nothing, 10% by default, so tiny metric changes don't cause scaling.
An HPA setting: before scaling down, it uses the highest replica count recommended during the window (300 seconds by default), so a short dip in load doesn't remove pods that will be needed again.
A periodic check Kubernetes (or a load balancer) runs against a container, such as an HTTP request to /healthz, to judge whether it is ready for traffic or needs restarting.
A Linux kernel feature that gives a group of processes its own network interfaces, IP address and routing. All containers in one pod share one, so they reach each other on localhost.
A named group within a Kubernetes cluster used to separate resources, names and policies, for example per team or environment.
A Kubernetes component that adds nodes (machines) when pods can't be scheduled for lack of room, and removes under-used nodes.
An open-source Kubernetes node autoscaler, originally built by AWS, that provisions right-sized nodes directly when pods are waiting to be scheduled.
Rolling-update settings on a Kubernetes Deployment: maxSurge is how many extra pods may exist above the desired count, and maxUnavailable is how many may be unavailable, during a rollout.
example: With 10 replicas, maxSurge 2 and maxUnavailable 0, the rollout keeps at least 10 available and at most 12 non-terminating pods.

definition: Running the new version (green) fully alongside the old (blue) and switching all traffic at once, keeping blue ready for a fast switch back.
Stopping a server without dropping work: stop accepting new requests, finish the ones in flight, then exit.
A request that a server has accepted but not yet finished answering.

The Unix signal asking a process to terminate. A well-behaved server catches it, stops taking new work and drains in-flight requests before exiting. Kubernetes sends it first when stopping a container.
The Unix signal that kills a process immediately; it cannot be caught or ignored. Kubernetes sends it when a container is still running after its termination grace period.
A command or HTTP call Kubernetes runs inside a container just before sending it the stop signal, often used to wait a few seconds while endpoint removal reaches the load balancers.
How long Kubernetes lets a terminating pod shut down (30 seconds by default) before force-killing it with SIGKILL. The preStop hook and draining share this budget.
The Kubernetes agent on every node. It starts and stops the containers for the pods assigned to that node and runs their probes.
The Kubernetes component on each node that programs packet-forwarding rules (iptables, IPVS or nftables) so traffic to a Service's virtual IP reaches one of its ready pods.
The list of pod IP addresses and ports behind a Service, stored in EndpointSlice objects, with flags saying which are ready. Routing components watch it to know where to send traffic.
A JavaScript runtime for running servers outside the browser, built on Google's V8 engine and an event loop.
A short, heavily promoted sale that causes a sudden, predictable spike in traffic.
A database of the currently available instances of each service and their addresses, kept up to date as instances start, stop and fail health checks.
A discovery pattern in which each service instance registers itself with the service registry on start-up and sends heartbeats to stay listed.
A discovery pattern in which the platform (for example Kubernetes, from pod readiness) registers and deregisters instances, rather than the instances themselves.
Netflix's open-source service registry, used with client-side discovery in Spring Cloud applications.
Netflix's client-side load-balancing library, used with Eureka; it is now in maintenance mode.
A discovery pattern in which the calling service asks the registry for the list of instances and chooses one itself. It avoids an extra hop but needs a discovery library in every language.
A discovery pattern in which the client calls one stable address, and a load balancer or router looks up the registry and forwards the request to an instance.
The long-standing Linux tool for packet filtering and address rewriting rules in the kernel; kube-proxy can use it to forward Service traffic.
A load balancer built into the Linux kernel; kube-proxy's IPVS mode uses it to spread Service traffic across pods efficiently in large clusters.
The modern successor to iptables in the Linux kernel's packet-filtering framework; kube-proxy has an nftables mode.
A Linux kernel technology that runs small, verified programs inside the kernel, used for fast networking, observability and security without kernel changes.
An open-source Kubernetes networking plugin that uses eBPF and can replace kube-proxy.
Software that gives Kubernetes pods their network connectivity, following the Container Network Interface (CNI) standard.
A Kubernetes Service setting that includes pods in DNS and endpoints even before they pass their readiness probe.
The package of tools and runtime for developing Java programs; new versions change defaults such as DNS caching.
The Java security property that sets how long successful DNS lookups are cached in the JVM. A value of -1 caches forever; historically, installing a security manager made the default "forever".
A systems programming language focused on memory safety without garbage collection.
Regularly replacing TLS certificates with new ones before they expire, done automatically by a service mesh's control plane.
Moving a chosen percentage of requests from one version or location to another, for example 5% to version 2 during a canary release.
Telling work that started on someone's behalf to stop because its result is no longer wanted. It is cooperative: the work has to check for it, and it cannot undo effects already applied.
A substitute response used when a dependency fails, such as cached or generic recommendations instead of personalised ones.
A design where one node (or one owner) accepts all writes for a piece of data. It avoids write conflicts but caps write throughput at what that one writer can do.
The step-by-step strategy a database (or Spark) chooses for running a query: which indexes to use, the join order and algorithms. Reading it shows why a query is slow.
A Python web framework with a built-in ORM.
Naming data by a hash of its contents, so the name changes whenever the content changes. Such names can be cached forever because they never point to different bytes.
A stored, precomputed query result that must be refreshed when its source data changes, unlike a regular view, which reruns its query every time.
example: PostgreSQL's REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY rebuilds the result while readers keep seeing the old one.

definition: A named, saved query that behaves like a table but is recomputed every time it is read.
Updating a materialised view by applying only the changes in its source data, rather than recomputing the whole query.
An open-source columnar database for fast analytical queries. Its materialised views run on each insert into the source table.
The feed of posts from accounts a user follows, shown when they open the app.
A precomputed summary table, such as hourly or daily totals, so dashboards don't scan raw events.
Suggesting completions while the user is still typing. It needs very fast prefix lookups, often from precomputed suggestions or edge n-grams.
When one logical write causes many physical writes, for example fan-out to millions of timelines or LSM compaction rewriting data several times. Read amplification is the same for reads.
The field used to decide which shard or partition a row belongs to. A good one spreads load evenly and keeps the most common queries on one shard.
example: Sharding a chat app by conversation_id puts a whole conversation on one shard.

definition: Sending one query to every shard and merging the answers. It gets slower and more fragile as shards are added, because the query waits for the slowest one.
The number of distinct values a field has. A high-cardinality key (user ID) spreads load across many partitions; a low-cardinality one (country) does not.
A query, join or transaction that touches data on more than one shard. These need coordination and are much more expensive than single-shard ones.
One of many small shards (often thousands) mapped onto fewer physical servers. Rebalancing moves whole logical shards between servers instead of rehashing every key.
Changing how data is split across shards (more shards, different key or ranges) while the system runs, which means moving data. It is one of the hardest live migrations.
To spread a fixed cost across many operations, so each one pays only a small share.
PostgreSQL's bulk-loading command, which loads many rows from a file or stream far faster than individual INSERTs.
Combining many small updates in memory (say 137 page views over 5 seconds) and writing one total, trading freshness and crash safety for far fewer writes.
How fast consumers remove work from a queue, for example 5,000 messages per second.
When average arrivals exceed capacity for a long time. A queue cannot fix it: the backlog grows without limit until you add capacity or shed load.
The in-memory, sorted buffer where an LSM-tree store collects recent writes before flushing them to disk as an immutable sorted file.
An immutable on-disk file of key–value pairs sorted by key, produced when an LSM-tree store flushes its memtable.
Measurements recorded over time, such as metrics or sensor readings. It is mostly appended and usually queried and expired by time range.
A record of every money movement as its own entry (debit or credit); a balance is the sum of the entries. Appending entries avoids contention on a single balance row.
Accounting in which every transaction is recorded as equal debits and credits in at least two accounts, so the books always balance.
A shard or partition that gets far more traffic than the others, capping the whole system's throughput at what that one partition can handle.
A lookup table that records which shard (or cell) each key or tenant lives on, so data can be moved by updating the table rather than rehashing.
The smallest positive number that two or more numbers all divide into exactly. lcm(4, 5) = 20.
Google Cloud's object storage service.
Microsoft Azure's object storage service.
A self-hostable object storage server compatible with the S3 API.
Open-source distributed storage that offers object, block and file storage on your own hardware.

A named container for objects in object storage, with its own access policies and settings. S3 general purpose buckets use a flat key namespace; S3 Express One Zone directory buckets work differently.
A stored item in object storage: the bytes plus metadata, addressed by a key within a bucket.

The name that identifies an object within a bucket, such as avatars/42/photo.jpg. Slashes are just characters; a prefix is the start of the key, used for listing and, in S3, for scaling request rates.
The S3 operation that returns object keys in a bucket, filtered by prefix, in lexicographic order and in pages of up to 1,000.
A pricing and performance tier in object storage. Infrequent-access and archive classes such as S3 Glacier cost less to store but more, or take longer, to read.
The error S3 returns while it scales up to a sudden rise in request rate on a prefix. Clients should retry with backoff and ramp up gradually.
An S3 feature that stops objects being deleted or overwritten for a retention period (write once, read many). It is about retention, not about coordinating concurrent editors.
A bucket setting that keeps every version of an object, so overwritten or deleted data can be recovered.
Azure's name for handing a client a token or signed URL with restricted, time-limited access to one resource, like a car's valet key, instead of routing data through your servers.
The method AWS uses to sign API requests and presigned URLs with an access key. Presigned URLs signed this way can last at most 7 days.
AWS's system of users, roles and policies that decides who may do what. A role gives temporary credentials to whatever assumes it, such as an EC2 instance or ECS task.
Short-lived AWS keys plus a session token, issued by STS for a role. Anything signed with them, including a presigned URL, stops working when they expire.
The AWS service that issues temporary credentials, for example when a role is assumed.
Amazon Elastic Container Service: AWS's container orchestrator.

S3's way of uploading a big object as separately uploaded parts (5 MiB to 5 GiB each, up to 10,000 of them) that are stitched into one object when you complete the upload. Failed parts are retried alone.
example: A 4 GB file in 100 MB parts is uploaded as 40 parallel parts.

definition: An upload protocol that lets the client ask how many bytes the server already has and continue from there after a dropped connection.
An open protocol for resumable file uploads over HTTP.
The server or bucket that holds the original content behind a CDN. The CDN fetches from it on a cache miss.
A way to serve private content through a CDN: the CDN only serves a request carrying a valid signature you issued, so content is cached at the edge but still access-controlled.
An object name that is never reused for different content (for example one containing a version or content hash), so it can be cached for a very long time without invalidation.
Streaming video as short segments in several renditions and letting the player switch rendition for each segment as bandwidth changes, so playback starts fast and rarely stalls.
Apple's adaptive streaming protocol: a .m3u8 playlist lists renditions and their short media segments, which players fetch over ordinary HTTP.
Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP: the international-standard (ISO/IEC 23009-1) counterpart to HLS.
A short chunk (typically 2–10 seconds) of a streamed video rendition, fetched as its own file.
Shorthand for picture size: "1080p" is 1,080 lines high (1920 × 1080 pixels), and 4K usually means 3840 × 2160.
High Efficiency Video Coding, a video compression standard that needs roughly half the bitrate of the older H.264 for similar quality.
Software or hardware that compresses (encodes) and decompresses (decodes) video, following a standard such as H.264, HEVC or AV1.

A keyframe is a video frame stored complete; the frames after it are stored as differences. A group of pictures (GOP) runs from one keyframe to the next, so video can only be split cleanly at keyframes.
Third-generation mobile data networks. Real-world speeds are typically from a few hundred kilobits to a few megabits per second, far below 4G or 5G.
Modern image formats that compress photos much smaller than JPEG at similar quality.
Encryption the storage service applies to data when it writes it to disk and removes when you read it. SSE-S3 uses keys S3 manages.
The SQL operator for simple pattern matching, where % matches any run of characters. A pattern starting with % usually cannot use an ordinary index, so the database scans every row.
A database's rules for comparing and sorting text, including whether uppercase and lowercase count as equal.
A search data structure that maps each term to the list of documents containing it (its posting list), often with positions and counts. It lets the engine jump straight to matching documents.
example: wireless → [1, 2] and mouse → [2, 3], so documents with both are [2].

definition: An index that maps each document to the words it contains; the opposite direction to an inverted index.
The sorted list of document IDs (and often positions and frequencies) stored for one term in an inverted index.

The sorted list of every distinct term in an inverted index, each pointing to that term's posting list. Lucene stores the terms in on-disk blocks and keeps a compact finite-state transducer (FST) in memory that maps term prefixes to the right block.

A compact automaton that maps input strings to outputs. Lucene uses one as its term index: it maps term prefixes to the on-disk blocks of the term dictionary, so a lookup needs little memory and few disk reads.
The open-source Java search library that implements inverted indexes, analysis and scoring. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr are built on it.
Combining terms with logic: AND keeps documents containing every term (intersect the posting lists), OR keeps documents with any (union).
The pipeline that turns text into the terms stored in a search index: a tokeniser plus token filters such as lowercasing and stemming. Queries must be analysed compatibly or they won't match.
The first step of text analysis: splitting text into tokens (usually words) at spaces and punctuation, or by dictionary or n-grams for languages written without spaces.
One unit of text produced by a tokeniser, such as a word; after filtering it becomes a term in the index.
A step in text analysis that changes the stream of tokens: lowercasing, ASCII folding (café → cafe), stemming, adding synonyms or removing stop words.
Reducing words to a common root so that variants match, for example running and runs to run.
Very common words such as the, a and for that are often dropped during analysis because they carry little meaning.
A configured equivalence such as tv ↔ television, applied during analysis so a query for one word finds the other.
The 7-bit character set of 128 English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes. ASCII folding converts accented characters to their nearest ASCII equivalents.
A run of n consecutive characters (or words). Edge n-grams are prefixes of a word (h, he, hea, head ...), indexed so search-as-you-type is a plain term lookup at the cost of a larger index.
In search, a token made of several consecutive words (a word n-gram), used for phrase-like matching.
How well a document matches what the searcher wanted, estimated by a scoring function such as BM25 and used to order results.
The whole collection of documents being searched.
How many times a term appears in a document or field. More occurrences suggest the document is more about that term.
A weight that is large for terms found in few documents and small for terms found everywhere, commonly log(N / df), where N is the number of documents and df the number containing the term.
example: In a million documents, a term in 1,000 of them gets log10(1,000) = 3; a term in 100,000 gets 1.

definition: A classic relevance weight: term frequency multiplied by inverse document frequency, rewarding terms that are frequent in this document but rare in the collection.

The default relevance function in Lucene-based search engines. It improves on TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation (controlled by k1, default 1.2) and field-length normalisation (controlled by b, default 0.75).
example: With k1 = 1.2, ten occurrences of a term score under twice as much as one.

definition: Repeating a search term many times in a document to try to rank higher. BM25's saturation reduces the reward for it.
Search that matches the actual tokens in the text, with no understanding of meaning, so sofa won't find couch unless a synonym is configured.
Search that represents queries and documents as embeddings and finds the nearest ones by meaning rather than by matching words.
A list of numbers produced by a machine-learning model to represent a piece of text or an image, positioned so that similar meanings are close together.
Combining lexical (BM25) and vector search results into one ranking, often followed by re-ranking with a learned model.
Re-scoring the top results from a cheap first search with a more expensive model to improve the final order.
A multiplier that makes matches in one field (such as the title) count more than matches in another.
How Elasticsearch picks a document's shard: by hashing its routing value (its _id by default) onto the primary shards. Because of this the primary count can't simply change later.
The node in an Elasticsearch cluster that manages cluster state, such as which shards live where, and promotes replicas when a primary fails.
Elasticsearch's traffic-light status: green means all shards are assigned, yellow means some replicas are not (data is still available), red means a primary is missing.
The Elasticsearch node that receives a search, sends it to a copy of every relevant shard, merges their results and fetches the winning documents.
The first step of a distributed search: each shard finds and returns only the IDs and scores of its own top results to the coordinating node.
The second step of a distributed search: after merging the global top results, the coordinating node fetches just those documents from their shards.
An Elasticsearch feature (on by default since 7.0) that sends each search to the shard copy expected to respond fastest, based on response times and queue sizes.
Elasticsearch's way to page deeply: instead of skipping results with from and size (capped at 10,000 by default by index.max_result_window), you pass the sort values of the last result you saw.
An Elasticsearch handle that freezes the index's state for a series of searches, so deep paging sees a consistent view.
Elasticsearch's per-shard write-ahead log. Indexed operations are recorded in it so they survive a crash before the next Lucene commit.

The operation that turns recently indexed documents into a new searchable segment. By default Elasticsearch refreshes every second, but only on indexes that have received a search in the last 30 seconds, so new documents become searchable shortly after indexing.
Writing all in-memory index data to disk as a durable Lucene commit, after which the translog can be trimmed.
Elasticsearch policies that automatically roll over to a new index (for example daily, or by size) and move or delete old indexes, used for logs and other time-based data.
An Elasticsearch option where you supply each document's version number; writes with an equal or lower version than the stored one are rejected, so older updates can't overwrite newer ones.
A second name that points to one or more Elasticsearch indexes. Applications query the alias, so you can build a new index and switch the alias to it atomically.
An Elasticsearch index's schema: each field's type and the analyser used for it.

The region of memory a Java program uses for the objects it creates while running. Its maximum size is configured (for example with -Xmx), and the garbage collector reclaims unused objects in it; a badly sized heap causes long garbage-collection pauses.
Waiting for a short pause (say 100–200 ms) before acting, so a burst of events such as keystrokes triggers only one request.
The set of systems a business uses to collect, store and analyse all its data, separate from the transactional databases: pipelines, a lake or warehouse, and batch and stream processing.
Bounded data has an end (yesterday's orders); unbounded data keeps arriving forever (a live event stream). Batch suits the first, streaming the second.
A data warehouse system on Hadoop that runs SQL queries as batch jobs.
Spark's stream-processing engine, which treats a stream as a continuously growing table.

Google's 2004 model for batch processing on clusters of cheap machines: a map step emits key–value pairs, a shuffle groups them by key, and a reduce step combines each key's values. Failed tasks are simply rerun.
The first MapReduce step: each worker reads a chunk of input and emits key–value pairs.
Redistributing intermediate data across the network so all values for a key reach the same worker. It is usually the most expensive part of a batch job.
The final MapReduce step: each reducer combines all the values for its keys, for example summing counts.
A pre-aggregation step on the mapper side that shrinks map output (say, summing counts locally) before the shuffle.
A file system spread over many machines that stores large files in replicated blocks, such as GFS or HDFS.
Google's distributed file system, described in a 2003 paper, which MapReduce read its input from.
The open-source ecosystem built around HDFS and a MapReduce implementation for batch processing on clusters.
Running a task on (or near) the machine that already stores its input, to avoid sending the data over the network.
A task that runs far slower than its peers, holding up the whole job. Frameworks run a backup copy on another machine (speculative execution) and use whichever finishes first.
A distributed processing engine that runs a DAG of transformations over partitioned data, keeping intermediate data in memory where it can; it handles batch, SQL, streaming and machine learning.
Spark's original core abstraction: an immutable, partitioned collection that remembers how it was computed so lost partitions can be rebuilt.
A distributed table with named columns in Spark, queried with SQL-like operations that the Catalyst optimiser can plan.
A graph of steps connected by one-way arrows with no loops. Spark plans a job as a DAG of transformations.
A group of Spark tasks that can run without moving data between machines; a shuffle starts a new stage.
One chunk of a distributed dataset, processed by one task. Spreading data evenly across partitions keeps tasks similar in length.
Deferring work until a result is actually needed. In Spark, transformations only build a plan; an action such as count or write runs it.
Spark SQL's query optimiser, which rewrites a DataFrame or SQL plan before running it, for example pushing filters down towards the data source and choosing join strategies.
The record of which earlier datasets and transformations produced a piece of data. Spark uses it to recompute lost partitions.

A narrow transformation (map, filter) builds each output partition from one input partition, so no data moves. A wide one (groupBy, join, repartition) needs data from many partitions and triggers a shuffle.
Joining a large dataset with a small one by sending a full copy of the small one to every worker, avoiding a shuffle of the large side.
A Spark join that avoids a shuffle because both tables are already stored partitioned compatibly on the join key.
A Spark feature that re-optimises a query while it runs using real statistics, for example merging tiny partitions or splitting skewed ones in joins.

A way to cut an endless stream into finite chunks for aggregation: tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, sliding (hopping) windows overlap, and session windows close after a gap of inactivity.
example: A 10-minute window sliding every minute counts orders in the last 10 minutes, updated each minute.

definition: Data a stream job remembers between events, such as running counts per key or open windows. It must be checkpointed so it survives failures.

A data architecture, described by Nathan Marz in 2011, that runs a batch layer (accurate recomputation over all history) and a speed layer (fast results for recent data) side by side, merged by a serving layer. Its main cost is maintaining the same logic twice.
An early open-source stream processor, created by Nathan Marz at BackType and later used at Twitter.
Kafka's ability to move older log segments to cheaper remote storage such as S3, so topics can retain much longer history.
Running data through a pipeline again, for example replaying a log through a fixed job, or backfilling results for historical data.
A processing engine (such as Spark, Beam or Flink) where the same code can run in batch or streaming mode.
Managed cloud data warehouses from Snowflake Inc., Google Cloud and AWS respectively.
Storing each row's values together, which suits transactional reads and writes of whole records but forces analytical queries to read every column.
A data lake with a table format on top, giving warehouse-like features (atomic commits, schemas, time travel) over files in object storage.

A metadata layer, such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake or Apache Hudi, that tracks which data files make up each snapshot of a table, so engines get atomic commits, schema evolution and consistent reads over a data lake.
A plain-text table format with one row per line and fields separated by commas.
A registry of a platform's tables and datasets: where they live, their schemas and owners. Table formats rely on one to find each table's current metadata.
Querying a table as it was at an earlier snapshot, which table formats support while old snapshots are retained.
Workloads of many small, concurrent reads and writes of individual records, such as placing orders, served by operational databases.
A common layering of lake tables: bronze holds raw data, silver cleaned and conformed data, gold business-level aggregates.
Loading raw data into the warehouse or lakehouse first and transforming it there with SQL, made practical by cheap storage and elastic compute.
A tool for writing and running SQL transformations inside a warehouse, with tests and documentation.
An open-source distributed SQL query engine that queries data where it lives, including lakehouse tables.
Original size divided by compressed size; a ratio of 5 means the data takes a fifth of the space.
Plans and systems for restoring service and data after a major failure, such as losing a whole region, measured against RPO and RTO.
Designing a system so it keeps working through a failure without needing to make changes, such as provisioning new capacity, during the event.
A load balancer or DNS service that sends each user to a healthy region, often the nearest one by measured latency.
The one region that owns a user's or tenant's data and accepts its writes; other regions forward writes there.
Splitting data by geography so each partition lives (and is written) in the region of its users.
Replication where several nodes or regions accept writes to the same data and exchange them, so concurrent conflicting writes must be resolved.
Dividing a system into many independent, identical copies (cells), each serving a subset of customers with no shared state, so a bad deploy or runaway customer affects only one cell.
The share of users or systems affected when something fails. Cells, staged deploys and shuffle sharding all shrink it.
Rolling a change out to one cell, region or small group first and widening it in waves only while it stays healthy.
Azure's name for deploying many independent copies (stamps) of an application, each serving a group of tenants: the same idea as cells.
Giving each customer a random small combination of workers from a large pool, so any two customers rarely share all of theirs and one bad customer harms very few others.
example: With 4 of 100 workers each, there are 3,921,225 possible combinations.

definition: The number of ways to pick k items from n when order doesn't matter: n! / (k! × (n − k)!).
The product of all whole numbers from 1 up to n, written n!; for example 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
An Azure pattern of deploying identical backend nodes in many regions, each able to serve any user, over a globally replicated data store.
A failure of the management systems that create, configure or scale resources, even while running workloads keep serving.
Short for coder-decoder: software or hardware that compresses and decompresses media, such as the H.264 or HEVC video codecs.

The two consistency modes of DynamoDB global tables. MREC (multi-Region eventual consistency, the default) replicates asynchronously, usually within a second, and resolves concurrent writes to an item with last-writer-wins. MRSC (multi-Region strong consistency) replicates each write synchronously to at least one other Region before acknowledging it, so strongly consistent reads in any Region see the latest version; a write that clashes with one in progress elsewhere fails and can be retried, instead of being silently overwritten.
A common abbreviation for Elasticsearch, the Lucene-based distributed search engine.
The Redis sorted-set command that returns a member's zero-based rank counting from the highest score, in O(log N) time where N is the number of members. Add 1 to show a 1-based position.
example: If a player has the third-highest score, ZREVRANK returns 2.

definition: In AWS Elastic Load Balancing, a named set of targets (instances, IP addresses or containers) that a load balancer routes requests to and health-checks.

In Elasticsearch, a copy of a primary shard kept on a different node. It can answer searches, which adds read capacity, and is promoted to primary if the node holding the primary fails; every replica also has to index every document.

A DynamoDB update action that adds a number to a numeric attribute (creating it if missing) or adds elements to a set, in one atomic step. It is not idempotent: retrying an ADD whose first attempt actually succeeded applies the increment twice, which is why AWS generally recommends SET.
